summaries.example: Imagine you are choosing a game to play. In the real situation, you choose chess. But you can also think about other ways things could go: you choose soccer, or you play with a different friend. These imagined ways are not all real places. They help us talk about what could happen and what must happen.
summaries.summary: The idea of a possible world helps philosophers discuss ways reality might have been different. Our actual world is one complete way things are. Other possible worlds represent different complete ways things could be. In modal logic, “necessarily” means true in every possible world, while “possibly” means true in at least one. The entry also explains that possible-world thinking helps with meanings, properties, and the difference between saying that something must be true of a particular thing and saying that a whole statement must be true. Philosophers then ask what worlds are. Some say they are concrete universes separate from ours. Others say they are abstract complete ways things could be. A third view says they are arrangements or combinations of objects and properties from the actual world.
key_ideas: We often think that reality could have been different in many ways.
In this approach, something is possible if it is true in at least one possible world, and necessary if it is true in every possible world.
Possible worlds help explain why a sentence can be true now without being necessarily true.
Philosophers disagree about what possible worlds really are: concrete universes, abstract descriptions, or recombinations of things in our world.
summaries.why_it_matters: Possible worlds give us a useful language for thinking about choices, rules, explanations, and things that might have happened. They also show why the same words can behave differently in ordinary statements and statements about what must or could be true. Learning the idea helps us see how logic can organize questions about possibility without pretending that philosophers all agree on the answers.

important_terms.definition: A complete way things could be, including the way things actually are and other ways things might have been.
The one possible world that is the way things really are.
A word or idea used to talk about what could be, must be, or cannot be.
A careful method for explaining when sentences about possibility and necessity are true.

questions_to_think_about: If something could have happened, must there be a possible world where it happens?
Is a possible world a real place, an idea, or something else?
Can one person exist in more than one possible world?
What is the difference between “this is true” and “this had to be true”?

summaries.example: Suppose the statement “All of Jordan’s pets are mammals” is true because Jordan currently has two dogs. It does not follow that it is necessarily true. In another possible world, Jordan might have a pet bird or turtle. Possible-world semantics represents this by treating necessity as truth in every possible world and possibility as truth in at least one. The example also shows why modal logic is intensional: two statements can have the same truth value in the actual world but differ in what would be true across other worlds.
summaries.summary: Possible worlds are introduced as a tool for modal logic. A sentence is necessary when it is true in every possible world and possible when it is true in at least one. This treatment turns modal operators into something like universal and existential quantifiers over worlds. It explains why modal logic is intensional: two expressions can have the same actual extension yet differ in other possible worlds, so substitution can change the truth of a modal sentence. The framework also represents propositions, properties, and relations by how their extensions vary from world to world. It helps distinguish de re modality, concerning what a particular object could or could not be, from de dicto modality, concerning a whole statement. The metaphysical debate begins when philosophers ask what worlds are. Concretism identifies them with concrete maximal connected realities and uses counterparts rather than literal identity across worlds. Abstractionism identifies them with abstract total states of affairs, but its account treats modality as basic rather than reducing it to non-modal facts. Combinatorialism instead understands worlds as structured recombinations of objects, properties, and relations, though it faces difficulties about essential properties and genuinely different entities.
key_ideas: Possible-world semantics supplies a rigorous interpretation of the modal operators “necessarily” and “possibly.”
Modal logic is intensional because actual coextension does not guarantee that expressions can be freely substituted inside modal contexts.
Possible-world analysis can model intensions as functions from worlds to extensions, and it clarifies de re and de dicto modality.
Concretism, abstractionism, and combinatorialism offer different answers to what worlds are and what it means for something to exist in a world.
Concretism treats worlds as concrete and uses counterparts to analyze claims about what an individual could have been.
Abstractionism usually treats worlds as abstract states of affairs and often combines this with actualism, the view that everything that exists is actual.
summaries.why_it_matters: The entry connects formal logic with metaphysics. Possible-world semantics explains how modal reasoning can be given precise truth conditions, while the competing metaphysical views reveal the costs of different explanations. The debate concerns questions that appear in theories of identity, necessity, properties, counterfactual reasoning, and what kinds of entities a philosophical theory should accept.

important_terms.definition: A logic in which the truth of some sentences depends on more than the actual extensions of their component terms or predicates.
The referent of a term, the things a predicate applies to, or the truth value of a sentence.
The meaning or sense of an expression; in possible-world semantics, often modeled as what an expression contributes across worlds.
A formal account that interprets necessity as truth at every possible world and possibility as truth at some possible world.
A property a thing has in every possible world in which it exists, rather than merely in the actual world.
A distinction between necessity concerning a particular object and necessity concerning a statement or description.
The view that possible worlds are concrete, maximally connected physical realities, with other worlds just as real as ours.
The view that possible worlds are abstract, complete, and consistent ways things could be.

questions_to_think_about: Does explaining possibility with possible worlds clarify modality, or merely restate it?
Should a theory of possible worlds include concrete alternate universes, abstract entities, or only actual objects and properties?
Why might a philosopher prefer counterpart relations to identity across worlds?
Can a theory remain actualist while explaining claims about individuals that might have existed but do not actually exist?
Are possible-world intensions too coarse if two expressions are true in exactly the same worlds?

summaries.example: Think about a school play. The actual play has a certain cast, script, and ending. But several other complete versions are easy to imagine: a different student gets the lead, the ending changes, or the play is never performed. A possible world is not just one small change; it is a whole way the story could be. A claim is possible if it is true in at least one complete version and necessary if it is true in every complete version.
summaries.summary: Possible-world theory begins with a familiar thought: the actual world could have been different. History, objects, and events might have developed in other ways, but each complete alternative would still be a whole world. In modal logic, necessity is represented by truth in every possible world, while possibility is represented by truth in at least one. This approach also explains why modal logic is not fully extensional. Two descriptions may apply to the same things in the actual world, yet replacing one with the other inside a claim about necessity can change the result. Possible-world semantics handles this by tracking how meanings, or intensions, work across worlds. It also distinguishes de dicto claims about a statement from de re claims about a particular object. The entry then examines three broad pictures. Concretism says worlds are concrete, maximally connected realities and that objects in different worlds are related by counterpart relations. Abstractionism says worlds are abstract, complete states of affairs; it usually accepts that the actual world has a special status and that everything that exists is actual. Combinatorialism says possible worlds arise from recombining objects, properties, and relations, but must explain why some combinations are impossible and how essential properties work.
key_ideas: Possible worlds let philosophers compare reality with ways it might have been.
“Necessary” and “possible” can be explained using every-world and some-world tests.
A sentence’s being true now does not guarantee that it is necessary.
Possible-world semantics helps explain why meanings matter, not just present facts.
Philosophers disagree about whether worlds are concrete, abstract, or built by recombining actual ingredients.
These theories also disagree about whether the same individual can exist in several worlds.
summaries.why_it_matters: Possible worlds are useful because they turn vague questions about “what could have happened” into a structured philosophical method. They also force us to examine hidden assumptions about meaning, identity, existence, and necessity. Comparing the theories teaches an important philosophical lesson: a powerful explanatory tool can still leave open deep questions about what its central objects really are.

important_terms.definition: A complete way reality could be, including the actual way things are and alternative ways they might have been.
The world that is not merely possible but is the complete way things really are.
A branch of logic that studies words such as “possibly” and “necessarily.”
The actual things a word refers to or a description applies to; for a sentence, its truth or falsity.
A meaning that can determine different extensions in different possible worlds.
The idea that something is true in every possible world where the thing exists.
The view that worlds are complete abstract ways things could be, rather than separate physical universes.
The view that worlds are concrete, complete physical realities, each with its own inhabitants.

questions_to_think_about: Is imagining a different situation enough to show that it is genuinely possible?
Why might two sentences that are both true now behave differently when we ask what is necessary?
Would a concrete-world theory be too costly, or does it explain more?
What advantages might an abstract-world theory have?
Could an object have a property by accident rather than essentially?
